claims.text: A temperature-activated change in deformation mechanism controls the stress–strain response of solution-treated HfNbTaTiZr from room temperature to 1250 °C.
The same temperature-activated mechanism controls the alloy's thermoelastic response over this temperature range.
Evolving local short-range chemical order produces temperature-dependent lattice distortions.
Solution-treated HfNbTaTiZr has a homogeneous chemical composition while retaining inherent chemical disorder.
The relevant structural mediator is temperature-dependent lattice distortion modulated by local short-range chemical order.
At lower temperatures, deformation is dominated by dislocation glide.
Lattice distortions are relatively low at lower temperatures.
Increasing temperature enhances lattice distortions originating from inherent chemical disorder.
Enhanced lattice distortions facilitate a transition toward diffusion-assisted dislocation creep.
The transition toward diffusion-assisted dislocation creep alters elastic moduli.
The transition toward diffusion-assisted dislocation creep alters thermal expansion behavior.
At 600 °C and above, elastic moduli will shift relative to room-temperature values.
At 600 °C and above, creep resistance will shift relative to room-temperature behavior.
Temperature-dependent changes in elastic moduli and creep resistance will correlate with increased lattice distortion and changes in local chemical order.
Diffraction will reveal systematic increases in lattice-parameter fluctuations or other distortion metrics as temperature rises.
Room-temperature deformation is predominantly dislocation glide, with distortions associated with chemical disorder minimally active.
The proposed mechanism applies from room temperature to 1250 °C under tensile loading in an inert environment.
Aging and severe cold rolling may involve additional mechanisms outside the stated hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism claims to link the reported aging effects, but the boundary states that aging may involve additional mechanisms not covered by the hypothesis.
